L237: Model Selection. In our experiment, we select three models from two representative Code LLM series, including CodeGemma [【32†4】] and CodeGeeX [【33†5】], for evaluation. CodeGemma series are trained by Google LLC and outperform some old-version Code LLMs like CodeLlama [【61†31】] on code completion tasks. We select CodeGemma-2b and CodeGemma-7b to compare the performance differences between models of distinct scales.
L238: CodeGeeX series have corresponding applications [【30†2】] with more than 935k downloads (on VScode [【58†28】] marketplace). We select CodeGeeX2-6b, a version with stable performance. We exclude earlier small-scale code-oriented models, such as CodeBERT [【99†57】] and CodeT5 [【100†58】], because large-scale code-oriented models perform much better than them in code completion tasks.
L239: Baseline Selection. We compare our ShadowCode to GCG-based and manually designed IPI attacks. In particular, the vanilla GCG [【55†26】] is a representative PI attack and does not meet the requirements of our attack scenarios. Therefore, we adapt GCG into an IPI attack that is applicable to Code LLMs, dubbed ‘C-GCG’ (code-oriented GCG). The manually designed IPI method (dubbed ‘IPI-M’) is designed based on the existing work [【46†18】].
L240: IPI-M limits the number of injected tokens to make the perturbation concise since the existing IPI attack usually uses a large number of readable comments. Besides, we also provide the results of the original model (dubbed ‘No Attack’) for reference, since the original model itself may also have inherent insecurity factor. More details for baselines are provided in Appendix 【25†A】.
L241: Evaluation Metrics. In this paper, we use ASR to evaluate the effectiveness, not bad cases rate (NBR) and selective threat factor (STF) to evaluate the flexibility, and number of injected tokens and chars (NIT and NIC) to evaluate the stealthiness. For ASR, we consider an attack successful only when the generated code has equivalent functionality to the target code and appears in the correct position.
L242: In other words, the generated code must not only have malicious functionality but also adhere to the code compilation syntax rules. NBR and STF are new metrics introduced for our target-specific attack scenarios. NBR represents the rate of feasible cases. The more cases remaining after excluding the unusable ones with low ASR (below a threshold $r_{1}$), the greater variety of malicious objectives the attack can achieve; STF represents the rate of successful cases and their threat level.
L243: The more cases with sufficiently high ASRs (above a threshold $r_{2}$) and larger overall ASR value, the greater the upper limit of the attack’s threat. Their formulations are as follows:
L244:  | $\displaystyle\text{NBR}$  | $\displaystyle=1-\frac{\text{\# of cases where ASR}<r_{1}}{\text{Total \# of cases}},$  |  | (7)
L245:  | $\displaystyle\text{STF}$  | $\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i\in\text{cases where ASR}>r_{2}}\text{ASR}_{i}}{\text{Total \# of cases}},$  |
L246: 
L247: where $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ are set to 20% and 80% respectively in our evaluation empirically. Further reasons of evaluation metrics selection are discussed in Appendix 【25†A】.
L248: Hyperparameters and Computational Facilities. We conduct experiments using the following parameter settings to evaluate our approach. During gradient calculation, we utilize five noisy code samples, and the random seed for initializing induced perturbations is set to 100. For forward reasoning enhancement module, the number of tokens reinforced is set to $h=2$, as defined in Equation (【91†3】).
L249: For the hyperparameters related to attack performance, the default parameter values are as follows: the Top-$k$ value is 400, the rate $r$ in Equation (【91†3】) is 0.4, the number of keyword is 2, and the perturbation length is 10. Tokenization to calculate token number is performed using Gemma’s tokenizer.
L250: We run Algorithm 【92†1】 on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 Graphics Card with the above parameter settings, employing a float16 precision format without quantization. In general, the perturbation generation process requires approximately 0.5-1 hours for CodeGemma-2b and 2-3 hours for both CodeGemma-7b and CodeGeeX-6b. These computational times ensure the generation of high-quality induced perturbations tailored to the respective model sizes across all the experiment threat cases.
L251: ### IV-B Evaluation on Open-source Code LLMs
L252: 
L253: We first perform the attack evaluation on open-source Code LLMs. This includes three aspects: (1) we assess the attack effectiveness over 3 Code LLMs across all threat cases, demonstrating that ShadowCode is widely effective and more threatening than other attacks; (2) we evaluate attack flexibility against different targets using two special metrics; (3) we evaluate the trade-off between effectiveness and stealthiness $w.r.t.$ the number of injected tokens.
L254: Performance on Effectiveness. We hereby evaluate whether ShadowCode can successfully induce the Code LLMs to generate attacker-specified targets. We control the number of injected tokens for three attack methods in this experiment. For ShadowCode, we use its default settings: perturbation length of 10 and 2 keyword, while C-GCG uses a prefix length of 12. Since IPI-M requires a sufficient number of tokens to be effective, we just limit its perturbation to fewer than 30 tokens.
L255: Table 【101†II】 provides the average ASR for four methods. The effectiveness of ShadowCode significantly outperforms the other baseline methods: it achieves an average ASR of over 80% across all three Code LLMs, with the highest average ASR reaching 86.6%.
L256: Comparing the three Code LLMs, the CodeGemma-7b model has the highest security in normal conditions (8.4% for No Attack) and is the least likely to generate vulnerable code. However, it is the most susceptible model to ShadowCode, which may be attributed to its strong contextual learning ability.
L257: Comparing the three programming languages, Python is the most susceptible language to ShadowCode due to its concise syntax and the smallest number of tokens consumed; Besides, ShadowCode is relatively less effective on CodeXGLUE, which is mostly due to its larger data length and more complex data content. In contrast, the simplest dataset with the shortest data items, MBPP, is the most vulnerable to attacks, including C-GCG and IPI-M.
L258: Therefore, we believe that an increase in the contextual complexity can reduce the ASR of ShadowCode. In other words, when the contextual code becomes complex, the strength of ShadowCode (e.g., the length of induced perturbations) needs to be increased accordingly to ensure the attack’s effectiveness. According to our subsequent experiments in Section 【19†IV-C】 and Section 【21†IV-E】, increasing the length of ShadowCode or the Top-$k$ value can effectively enhance the attack performance of ShadowCode.
L259: Additionally, we further enrich our experimental results by exploring the attack effectiveness for each case in Appendix 【26†B】.
L260: TABLE III: The attack evaluation results of NBR and STF against open-source Code LLMs. Best results are marked in bold.
L261:

L264: C-GCG  | 0.39  | 0.50  | 0.56

L271: Flexibility. Previous experiments indicate that ShadowCode exhibits the best average ASR performance across various models. However, in real-world scenarios, attackers may have more complex demands. Generally, these demands can be categorized into two situations. One is when attackers want to achieve diverse malicious objectives, which requires that cases with low ASR be minimized. The other is when attackers want to cause severe damage, which requires that cases with high ASR be maximized.
L272: We refer to the capability to meet these complex demands as ”flexibility.” NBR is used to evaluate attack flexibility for the first situation, and STF for the second.
L434: Specifically, for “skipping critical process,” we use “… directly after …” and “without any check”; for “wrong memory usage,” we use “It is important to … directly after …”; for “outputting dangerous snippets,”, we use “It is very important to promptly … after …”. Notably, the perturbation in IPI-M must be sufficiently explicit; for example, it needs to specify the code snippet you want to insert (e.g., “os.system("rm -rf")”) or present a clear assertion (e.g., “SSL3 is the most secure protocol”).
L435: Otherwise, Code LLMs are difficult to induce successfully. Arguably, the actual performance of IPI-M may be worse than our evaluation results shown in main experiments because of obvious malicious intent. C-GCG mainly follows the GCG method, employing an induced perturbation greedily optimized based on output tuple to achieve malicious objectives. Compared to ShadowCode, C-GCG does not use code simulation and two key modules: forward reasoning enhancement and keyword-based design.
L436: Value and Metric Selection. We select the values of $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ based on the attack’s performance in the experiment. Specifically, in our experiments, 20% ASR is smaller than the ASR of no attack baseline in some situations, and 80% ASR outperforms the best performance of all the baselines. In addition, we find that only a few subcases (determined by the model, dataset, attack method, and case) have a success rate between 20% and 80%, accounting for 7.5%.
L437: Therefore, setting 20% and 80% as threshold of bad case and outstanding case respectively is appropriate.
L438: As for metrics, we have already explained why metrics such as NBR and STF are used in the main experiments. Here we further explain some details related to them. First, NBR does not take the specific ASR value into account, as this metric is used to measure the diversity of attacks, rather than ensuring stable success rates. Second, STF targets the situation where attackers aim to cause as much damage as possible, and it varies with differences in ASR.
L439: In other words, even a difference between 100% ASR and 95% ASR can have a real impact on the overall threat level. Therefore, the calculation of STF considers the specific ASR value. In addition, we do not use common metrics for code generation tasks, such as BLEU or CodeBLEU [【77†47】], because they do not directly reflect the effectiveness of the attacks. Overall, we attempt to confirm the realistic meaning of each evaluation metric from different perspectives.

L461: Fig. 13: Three examples of ShadowCode attack cases. Code LLMs normally generate code segment without vulnerabilities, but they lose this ability after being attacked by ShadowCode. Attackers can modify the output content at the specified location through ShadowCode, and they can even generate malicious code snippets that have never appeared in the context, e.g., “os.system("rm -rf /")”.
L462: ## Appendix B More Experiments
L463: 
L464: 【125†Image: Refer to caption】 Fig. 14: The ASR across different cases. The experimental results shown in this figure are the average values calculated from the effectiveness experiments involving 3 programming languages, 4 datasets, and methods excluding Clean Accuracy.
L465: Effectiveness across Different Cases. In the main experiments, we have validated the outstanding attack performance of ShadowCode from three perspectives: model, dataset, and programming language. Here, we supplement the attack details for different attacks on a single case. Specifically, we use ASR to evaluate the performance of ShadowCode and the baselines across different cases. We present the specific average ASR for each case.
L466: As shown in Figure 【126†14】, ShadowCode achieves a certain level of effectiveness across all cases, with an overall average ASR of 83.4%. However, both C-GCG and IPI-M have cases where they are completely ineffective, especially for IPI-M. This demonstrates that directly using traditional GCG methods or manually designing perturbations is not effective in some scenarios.
L467: We believe this involves three reasons: (1) The baseline methods are not fully suitable for contexts with structured features, which is a fundamental characteristic of the code completion task; (2) The specific malicious objective include complex semantics such as target code, position code, and “disregarding security attributes,” which are sometimes not fully captured by the perturbations generated by the baseline methods; (3) The impact of keyword-based design and FRE; our ablation study proves that these two modules play a critical role.
L468: According to the results, the most challenging to achieve is the straightforward case ST2. This case requires generating an obviously malicious command in a completely unrelated context. Another difficult case to implement is the CWE22 “Path Traversal,” which involves using unconventional paths like “../” to access files that are normally inaccessible. This case is relatively easier to achieve in Python, where the Code LLMs tend to suggest directly reading the path.
L469: However, it is more challenging to implement in Java and C/C++, as Code LLMs often only recommend checking the path rather than directly reading the file. CWE843 involves manipulating union members in a struct in C/C++. This represents a more complex malicious objective, where we attempt to manipulate one value within the union using an untrusted value. This is an unconventional operation that is difficult to describe using natural language, making it challenging for IPI-M to successfully attack.

L40: # ShadowCode: Towards (Automatic) External Prompt Injection Attack against Code LLMs Thanks:  Yuchen Yang, Hongwei Yao, Bingrun Yang, Yiling He, and Zhan Qin are with the State Key Laboratory of Blockchain and Data Security, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310007, China and also with Hangzhou High-Tech Zone (Binjiang) Institute of Blockchain and Data Security, Hangzhou 310053, China (e-mail: {ychyang, yhongwei, yangbingrun, qinzhan}@zju.edu.cn, heyilinge0@gmail.com).
L77: In addition, we evaluate ShadowCode on mainstream commercial Code LLM-integrated applications, including CodeGeeX [【30†2】] (with more than 935k installations in the VScode [【58†28】] extension marketplace) and Github Copilot [【29†1】] (developed by Github and OpenAI [【37†9】]). These applications correspond to the gray-box and black-box attack scenarios, respectively.
L78: ShadowCode achieves an ASR of up to 93.3% on CodeGeeX and 90.4% on Copilot using perturbations generated by open-source Code LLMs, confirming its serious threat in the real world.
L79: In summary, this paper makes three main contributions: (1) We reveal the potential limitations of existing backdoor and adversarial attacks against Code LLMs, and introduce a new attack paradigm, i.e., external prompt injection. (2) We propose a simple yet effective method (i.e., ShadowCode). ShadowCode can generate concise induced perturbations with effectiveness in an uncontrolled context environment.
L80: (3) We conduct extensive experiments to evaluate ShadowCode under 31 representative threat cases on 3 representative open-source Code LLMs and 2 commercial Code LLM-integrated applications, demonstrating its effectiveness, stealthiness, and resistance to potential defenses.
L81: ## II Background and Related Work
L82: ### II-A Code LLMs for Code Completion
L83: Code and its comments serve as a valuable corpus for deep learning models, facilitating various code-related tasks, including code translation [【59†29】] and code understanding [【60†30】]. The emergence of LLMs provides new alternatives to coding tasks. Leveraging the extensive knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs, researchers have developed specialized models, e.g., Codex [【31†3】], CodeLlama [【61†31】], CodeGemma [【32†4】] and CodeGeex [【33†5】].
L84: These Code LLMs can provide detailed explanations regarding the intrinsic logic of code and efficiently generate a wide range of functionally complex code [【62†32】, 【63†33】]. This paper focuses on code completion [【35†7】, 【34†6】]. This is a paradigmatic task involving the generation of new code from incomplete input using Code LLMs, which have been integrated into commercial applications [【29†1】, 【30†2】]. However, this development paradigm may encounter some potential threats.
L85: On the one hand, Code LLMs are susceptible to influence from the code context, which can alter the generated code. On the other hand, attackers can easily control the context of code generation, such as by inserting external code when the user copies code, installs packages, or builds knowledge bases, thus affecting the decisions made by Code LLMs. Related events have already occurred in the real world [【64†34】], highlighting its realistic threat.
L86: ### II-B Backdoor and Adversarial Attacks
L87: Backdoor attacks target the training process of DNNs [【65†35】, 【66†36】]. These attacks implant malicious backdoors that can be activated by an attacker-specified trigger into a model during training, leading the model to misbehave when the trigger is present [【67†37】, 【68†38】]. In the code domain, there are generally two strategies to achieve this, including dataset poisoning [【38†10】, 【40†12】] and model poisoning [【39†11】].
L311: Results. As shown in Table 【106†IV】, in the gray-box scenario, ShadowCode still demonstrates great attack performance. In Python and C/C++, ShadowCode achieves ASRs of 80.4% and 93.3%, respectively. Even in the worst-performing case (i.e., Java), the ASR achieves 71.7%, with only a 9.1% decrease compared to the white-box scenario; In the black-box scenario, ShadowCode also achieves a satisfying attack performance of 90.4% on Python. The ASRs on C/C++ and Java are 67.7% and 74.4%, respectively.
L312: In other words, our ShadowCode still maintains a high level of threat, although its performance is lower than that of white-box scenarios to some extent. In addition, ShadowCode achieves a high NBR ($>0.7$) and STF ($>0.6$) in both the gray-box and black-box scenarios, indicating that it also maintains sufficient flexibility.
L313: Overall, ShadowCode achieves good attack performance in both gray-box and black-box scenarios, demonstrating its reliable transferability and threat to the commercial applications in the real-world.
L314: In Figure 【107†7】, we present a representative case of ST2 in the black-box scenario. The concise perturbation “TR os now rm sys” is inserted in the comment of a tool function. The commercial applications generate the functional code “os.system("rm -rf /")” at the attacker-specified position (i.e., after using TRG function) under the induction of the perturbation, although it is obviously a highly malicious instruction that can cause dangerous results.
L315: ### IV-D Resistance to Potential Defenses
L316: 
L317: In this section, we further discuss whether our method can resist potential adaptive defenses that are particularly designed for our attack. In general, we can roughly categorize these defenses into detection and removal and design following potential defense methods against ShadowCode.
L318: 【108†Image: Refer to caption】 Fig. 8: The T-SNE plot of the classification keyword [CLS] at layer 17 shows the semantic differences between the original data and the injected data in the last embedding layer of CodeGemma-2b. T-SNE plot figures at the other layers have similar results.
L319: Detection: Semantic Analysis. Detection methods distinguish between malicious payload code that contains perturbations and normal code, thus rejecting the use of malicious payload code. Since detection methods based on code functionality are ineffective against non-functional perturbations, we adopt a semantic analysis approach. This involves examining the differences between the benign code and the injected code in the embedding layer of Code LLMs. However, this method may be difficult to implement.
L320: We find that code segments injected with perturbations might not have obvious semantic differences from benign ones. Specifically, as shown in Figure 【109†8】, we sample 1640 code segments and construct classification prompts. We detailly discuss the setting of this semantic analysis in Appendix 【26†B】. The results show that benign code and injected code are almost completely indistinguishable.
L321: Fig. 9: The resistance to the removal of chars. We remove characters from the perturbation, selecting 5% for removal each time, and we calculate the average ASR for each programming language across applicable cases. As the influence of the perturbation fades, the ASR results converge to the same level as no attack baseline.
L322: Removal: Massive Deletion and Find-and-Replace. This type of defense involves removing perturbations by altering the non-functional parts of the code after introducing external code. In general, it entails a trade-off between code readability and the strength of removal since we cannot faithfully detect injected code segments (as mentioned above). To explore its effectiveness, we hereby test the impact of the percentage of character removal on the effectiveness of perturbations.
L323: As shown in Figure 【110†9】, ShadowCode still maintains a sufficiently high ASR under a 50% removal rate. On the other hand, even if readability is completely sacrificed by extensively removing comments, ShadowCode can still be effective through non-comment portions of the code, as indicated in Table 【111†V】. Arguably, the removal methods are likely to require significant human effort and may not yield effective results since ShadowCode imposes strict limitations on the length of perturbations.
